lines: One real, small program gets built once, the ordinary way.
Then it gets built again, with one extra setting telling the compiler to optimize across the whole program at once. Does that second real build genuinely take longer?
answer: Optimizing across the whole program costs real linking time.

lines: Run it for real: the ordinary build and the whole-program build are both timed directly, and the whole-program one genuinely takes longer, every single time.
The identical program, built once the ordinary way, and once more with one setting telling the compiler to strip extra information out of the finished file.
Does the real file on disk actually get smaller?
answer: The real file on disk gets smaller.

lines: Run it for real: the ordinary file and the stripped file are both measured directly, and the stripped one is genuinely smaller every time, with the program's own behavior never touched at all.
steps.takeaway: A profile setting can shrink what actually ships without changing a single line of what the program does.

lines: Same program again, but this time the setting being changed is what happens when it panics: whether it unwinds the stack, or simply stops.
Does the real file on disk shrink this time too?
answer: The machinery for unwinding costs real space, even when nothing ever panics.

lines: Run it for real: the unwinding version and the stop-immediately version are both measured directly, and the one that simply stops is genuinely smaller every time, because it never had to carry that machinery at all.
steps.takeaway: A release profile's own settings trade away a real capability for a real, measured amount of space.

lines: One real, independent page names both of these exact ideas directly, in its own words.
It says whole-program optimization costs real linking time in exchange for better code, and that splitting a build into more parallel pieces can cost real speed in exchange for finishing faster.
steps.takeaway: Every one of these settings is a real trade made on purpose, never a free improvement with no cost at all.

lines: So here's what this topic's own three real settings are really standing in for: there is no single switch anywhere in here that just makes a program faster for free.
Optimizing across the whole program trades real time spent building for real speed once it runs.
Stripping extra information trades the ability to debug it easily for a smaller file that actually ships.
And changing how it panics trades away a real safety net for a little less space.
Every single one of them is a real decision someone has to make on purpose, not a box anyone should just tick without knowing what it costs.
